title: China's Deposit Insurance Fund is strikingly underfunded
gist: China's Deposit Insurance Fund held just RMB130bn at end-2025, an estimated 0.1% of ~RMB124tn insured deposits versus a 1.5% IMF-reported target and far below US (1.42%), EU (0.8%) and Japan (0.43%) levels, after bailouts like Baoshang drained it. Depositors are likely protected by implicit state support, but losses would be socialized onto the public balance sheet; Huang urges higher risk-based bank levies now and stricter bail-in rules.

insights.claim: China's Deposit Insurance Fund held only RMB130 billion ($18.5 billion) at end-2025, an estimated 0.1 percent of insured deposits, versus a 1.5 percent target reported by the IMF.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: China's bank-failure backstop is roughly 1/15th of its own target, so any sizable failure must be funded outside the prefunded pool.
insights.quote: At the end of 2025, its reported balance(link is external) was only RMB130 billion ($18.5 billion), equivalent to an estimated 0.1 percent of insured deposits
insights.locator: Body: China's Deposit Insurance Fund (DIF), a key pillar

insights.claim: Because Chinese authorities do not publish insured-deposit figures, Huang backs out insured deposits from the IMF's target (about US$224 billion / RMB1.6 trillion at a 1.5 percent ratio), implying RMB107 trillion insured, about 37 percent of RMB290 trillion total deposits at end-2023.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: A reusable method to estimate opaque deposit-insurance coverage; the 0.1 percent figure is an estimate that depends on the IMF target inputs.
insights.locator: Note 2: The IMF's 2025 Financial Sector Assessment Program

insights.claim: Carrying the 37 percent insured share forward to the People's Bank of China's reported RMB336 trillion of total deposits at end-2025 implies about RMB124 trillion of insured deposits in China.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Sizes the contingent liability: roughly RMB124 trillion of insured deposits sits behind a RMB130 billion fund.
insights.locator: Yet this relatively generous coverage is backed

insights.claim: By comparison, the US Deposit Insurance Fund's reserve ratio was 1.42 percent at end-2025 (above its 1.35 percent statutory minimum), the EU generally requires at least 0.8 percent, and Japan held 0.43 percent at end-March 2026, while Brazil and India have much higher ratios than many advanced economies.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: China's deposit-insurance prefunding is an outlier even versus Japan; useful benchmark for relative banking-system backstop strength.

insights.claim: The EU Deposit Guarantee Schemes Directive allows member states with highly concentrated banking sectors to target a lower 0.5 percent ratio, and France uses this derogation and meets the lower target.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Even the EU's lowest permitted target is five times China's estimated ratio.
insights.locator: Note 3: The EU Deposit Guarantee Schemes Directive

insights.claim: China's deposit insurance covers nearly 3,000 banks and protects up to RMB500,000 per depositor per bank, which the People's Bank of China says fully protects more than 99 percent of depositors.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Near-universal retail coverage means confidence rests on the state's backstop rather than the fund itself.
insights.locator: The system covers(link is external) nearly 3,000 banks

insights.claim: China's deposit insurance limit of about five times GDP per capita is among the most generous in the world, double the G20 median of 2.5 times GDP per capita reported by the International Association of Deposit Insurers for 2022.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: High coverage plus tiny prefunding maximizes the implicit fiscal guarantee on Chinese bank liabilities.
insights.locator: At about five times China's GDP per capita

insights.claim: Extensive use of China's Deposit Insurance Fund, including payments to creditors beyond deposit-insurance coverage, depleted its resources, and Chinese bank resolution remains heavily reliant on public funding without forcing creditors to absorb significant losses.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Creditor bail-in is weak in China, so senior/uninsured bank creditors have historically been protected by public money — a moral-hazard signal for bank credit pricing.
insights.quote: Bank resolution also remains heavily reliant on public funding and does not force creditors to absorb significant losses.
insights.locator: Generous coverage backed by a small fund

insights.claim: In the 2019 Baoshang Bank failure, all household deposits and other claims up to RMB50 million were fully protected (100 times the RMB500,000 statutory limit), and the Deposit Insurance Fund spent RMB93 billion in 2020, roughly three quarters of its reserves, on Baoshang alone, with the People's Bank of China adding further support.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: A single mid-sized regional bank failure consumed most of the fund — the DIF cannot absorb a multi-bank regional crisis without state money.
insights.locator: Note 1: For example, when Baoshang Bank failed in 2019

insights.claim: A low deposit-insurance reserve ratio in China does not necessarily mean insured depositors lose money, because recoveries from failed banks' assets, the Financial Stability Guarantee Fund set up in 2022, and central and local government resources can cover shortfalls.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Depositor run risk is low; the real risk transfer is to the sovereign/local-government balance sheet.

insights.claim: Expectations of government support likely explain why the tiny size of China's Deposit Insurance Fund has done little to undermine depositor confidence.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Chinese deposit stability is a function of perceived state guarantee, not prefunded insurance — watch for any erosion of that perception.
insights.locator: Indeed, expectations of government support may help

insights.claim: Little public information exists on the size or functions of China's Financial Stability Guarantee Fund, established in 2022, leaving its role as a bank-failure backstop opaque.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Opacity of China's second-line backstop makes bank-resolution capacity hard to model.
insights.locator: Chinese financial regulators established(link is external) a Financial Stability Guarantee Fund in 2022

insights.claim: A small deposit insurance fund forces China to raise money during financial stress, where hiking bank contributions strains banks when they are weakest and unrecovered government support socializes losses onto the public balance sheet and encourages bank risk-taking.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Expect either procyclical levies on Chinese banks in a crisis or rising contingent fiscal liabilities — both negative for bank equity or sovereign/LGFV credit.
insights.quote: it essentially socializes losses by shifting them onto the public balance sheet, which can encourage banks to take greater risks
insights.locator: The greater concern is who ultimately would bear

insights.claim: Huang argues Chinese regulators should require higher bank contributions to the Deposit Insurance Fund now, especially from riskier banks, while financial conditions are relatively stable, rather than during a future crisis.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: If adopted, risk-based premiums would raise costs for weaker regional/small banks, compressing their margins relative to large state banks.
insights.locator: China should rebuild the Deposit Insurance Fund

insights.claim: Huang recommends that replenishing China's Deposit Insurance Fund be paired with stricter limits on its use: shareholders and uninsured creditors bearing losses per the legal hierarchy, no protection beyond the statutory limit, cost-recovery mechanisms for government support, and clarity on the Financial Stability Guarantee Fund's role.
insights.speaker: Tianlei Huang
insights.so_what: Implementation would mean real bail-in risk for uninsured creditors of Chinese small banks — a repricing trigger for their interbank and bond funding.
insights.quote: Shareholders and uninsured creditors should bear losses in accordance with the legal hierarchy, while protection beyond the statutory coverage limit should be avoided.
insights.locator: China should reform the system in several ways.
